notes.meaning: John receives a measuring rod and is told to measure the temple, the altar, and the worshippers. In the Bible, measuring something shows that God claims it, evaluates it, and keeps it safe. The inner building represents God's true people and pure worship, protected by Him even during hard times.

differ.view: believe this foretells a literal Jewish temple that will be rebuilt in Jerusalem before Jesus returns, while others believe the temple symbolizes the true church.

notes.meaning: John is ordered to skip the outer courtyard because it has been left to the nations. These worldly forces will trample the holy city for forty-two months. This shows that while evil powers are allowed to oppress the visible religious world for a season, God sets a strict limit on their time.

differ.view: take the forty-two months as a literal three and a half years at the end of history, while others see it as a symbol for the entire time between Christ's first and second coming.

notes.meaning: God promises to give authority to two witnesses who will speak His word for 1,260 days. They wear sackcloth, which is coarse cloth worn by mourners, showing their deep sadness over the sins and distress around them. Even in seasons of great spiritual decline, God keeps faithful voices alive to speak His truth.

differ.view: believe the witnesses are two individual men who will preach during the final tribulation, while others believe they symbolize the faithful preaching church throughout history.

other.label: Orthodox
other.view: Many early church fathers held that the two witnesses are Enoch and Elijah, who were taken to heaven without dying and will return to preach before the end of the world.

notes.meaning: The two witnesses are described as olive trees and lampstands that stand before the Lord. This picture comes from the Old Testament book of Zechariah, where olive trees constantly supply oil to keep holy lamps burning. It shows that God's messengers do not rely on their own strength, but are continually filled with the power of the Holy Spirit to shine His light.

Anyone who tries to hurt these witnesses is destroyed by fire coming out of their mouths. This reminds readers of how God protected Elijah with fire, and how God made Jeremiah's words act like fire against his hearers. It means that the judgment these prophets declare carries God's own power to overcome their enemies.

The witnesses are given power to shut the sky so that no rain falls, to turn water into blood, and to strike the earth with plagues. These miracles echo the great works done through Elijah and Moses in the Old Testament. They show that God gives His servants full authority to confront a rebellious world and call people to repent.

When the witnesses finish their assigned message, a beast rising from the deep pit attacks them, overpowers them, and kills them. This evil power can touch them only after their work is fully done. God's servants are safely kept in His hands until they have carried out everything He called them to do.

The bodies of the two witnesses are left lying in the open street of the great city. The city is spiritually called Sodom for its sin and Egypt for its oppression, pointing to Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified. Refusing to bury them was the ultimate act of disrespect, showing deep hatred toward the messengers and their Lord.

People from all nations and language groups stare at the corpses for three and a half days and refuse to let them be buried. Leaving bodies in the street was considered a terrible humiliation in the ancient world. Yet this public shaming lasts only a brief time compared to the long season of their ministry.

The people living on earth celebrate the death of the witnesses as if it were a holiday, sending gifts to one another. They rejoice because they think they are finally free from the warnings that bothered their guilty consciences. When people love their sins, the plain truth of God feels like torment to them.

After three and a half days, God's breath of life enters the two fallen witnesses, and they stand back on their feet. Sudden dread falls upon everyone who sees them alive again. God proves that His truth cannot be killed and that He holds the ultimate power over life and death.

A loud voice from heaven calls out, telling the witnesses to come up. They rise into heaven in a cloud while their enemies watch. God publicly honors and rescues His faithful servants right in front of the very people who mocked and hated them.

At that very hour, a violent earthquake strikes the city, destroying a tenth of it and killing seven thousand people. The survivors are struck with terror and give glory to the God of heaven. Through this severe judgment, God compels people to recognize His majesty and authority.

The second woe, which covers the judgments of the sixth trumpet and the story of the witnesses, has now ended. The third and final woe is announced to be coming very soon. God's plan moves steadily forward without delay toward its final completion.

The seventh angel sounds his trumpet, and loud voices in heaven burst out in praise. They declare that the rule over the whole earth has now passed to God and His Messiah, Jesus Christ, who will reign forever. Even though evil once seemed to dominate the earth, God's rightful kingdom wins in the end.

The twenty-four elders sitting on their heavenly thrones fall on their faces to worship God. These leaders represent the whole company of God's redeemed people rejoicing in His victory. Even the highest rulers in heaven bow in deep humility before the living Lord.

The elders thank the Lord God Almighty, the One who is and who was, for stepping forward to rule openly. They do not say 'who is to come,' because He has now arrived in full power to take charge. God puts an end to human rebellion and shows that His authority has never failed.

Earthly nations showed their anger against God, but now God's righteous anger has arrived. The time has come to judge the dead, to reward all His servants and saints—both great and small—and to destroy those who ruin the earth. In the end, God makes every wrong right and faithfully rewards everyone who honors Him.

God's temple in heaven is opened wide, revealing the ark of His covenant. In Israel's history, the ark was the holy gold-covered chest that showed God's faithful presence and His promises to His people. Lightning, thunder, and a great hailstorm show the breathtaking glory of God and the holy judgment He sends against sin.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Some Catholic commentators view the ark in heaven as a image of the Virgin Mary, who carried Christ within her, linking this verse directly to the heavenly woman described in the next chapter.
